Adult Kasawala (Oreochromis squamipinnis) have been documented to reach a maximum total length of 36 centimeters [Li = 36 centimeters], a value that situates them among the larger-bodied cichlid species endemic to Lake Malawi. This species exhibits a relatively rapid somatic growth trajectory, with individuals attaining sexual maturation once they have reached a total length of 26.9 centimeters [Lp = 26.9 centimeters]. Field records from the southern lake basin indicate that the transition from a growing juvenile to a reproductively mature fish is closely tied to the attainment of this specific body size, after which energetic investment shifts increasingly toward reproductive functions. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a power-law scaling pattern comparable to that observed in other Oreochromis congeners, with the ultimate mass of a fully grown adult female estimated at approximately 737.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 737.4 grams] based on length-weight regressions derived from extensive sampling across multiple populations. The maximum recorded body mass attained by large, aged individuals under favorable lake conditions is consistent with this asymptotic value, though local food availability and population density can substantially modulate ultimate size.

At puberty, Kasawala individuals weigh approximately 309.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 309.5 grams], a mass that reflects the substantial energetic investment required to reach reproductive competence in a competitive lacustrine environment. This value was derived from a length-weight regression applied to the species' size at first maturation. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from demersal eggs at a remarkably small size, with the prolarva at the moment of eclosion weighing only 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams]. This minute wet weight at birth, equivalent to roughly 8.2 milligrams, represents a drastic contrast to the adult body mass and underscores the extreme ontogenetic size range this cichlid traverses during its development. The small size of the newly emerged larva is consistent with that predicted from an egg diameter of approximately 2.5 millimeters, a common oocyte size among mouthbrooding tilapiine cichlids. The initial body mass of the sac-fry constrains the duration of the yolk absorption stage, during which the endotrophic larva remains dependent on its endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding.

Maintained at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], reproductively active female Kasawala exhibit a maximum reproductive output that can be expressed in ecologically meaningful terms. Gravid individuals produce an average of approximately 2 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2 eggs per spawning event], and under continuous warm-water conditions, they can complete more than one spawning cycle annually, with field observations indicating roughly 1 spawning event per year [F_R_i = roughly 1 spawning event per year]. This annual reproductive schedule is typical of iteroparous cichlids with parental care. The combination of modest clutch sizes and infrequent spawning events reflects the substantial maternal investment associated with mouthbrooding, as each clutch must be incubated orally for an extended period before the fry are released. The species' reproductive strategy thus prioritizes offspring survival through intensive parental care over a high numerical output.

The lifespan of Oreochromis squamipinnis under natural lake conditions has been estimated at approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] at a constant water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a comparatively long maximum longevity for a cichlid of this body size. This estimate is based on mark-recapture studies and otolith increment analysis conducted in populations from the Nkhata Bay region. The extended adult lifespan permits multiple reproductive seasons, with females potentially spawning over several consecutive years. The species' maximum longevity of roughly 9 years [am = roughly 9 years] is notable among Malawi cichlids, many of which have shorter lifespans due to intense predation pressure from piscivorous fishes at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. In laboratory settings where individuals are maintained at a constant temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], captive Kasawala have been observed to survive for durations comparable to those recorded in the wild, suggesting that the nine-year figure is a robust estimate of the species' fundamental physiological longevity rather than an artifact of favorable field conditions.

Comparative morphometric analysis reveals that the relationship between length and body mass in Kasawala conforms closely to the scaling exponent typical of the genus Oreochromis, with the wet weight at puberty of 309.5 grams [Wwp = 309.5 grams] being achieved at the previously noted length of 26.9 centimeters [Lp = 26.9 centimeters]. The ultimate wet weight of 737.4 grams [Wwi = 737.4 grams] represents the maximum mass documented for large, aged females in stable lacustrine habitats. In the context of the Lake Malawi cichlid radiation, O. squamipinnis occupies a mid-sized ecological niche relative to its piscivorous and molluscivorous relatives. The species' total length at first maturation, documented at 26.9 centimeters [Lp = 26.9 centimeters], is consistent with the size at which gonadal recrudescence is initiated in related tilapiine species. These morphological benchmarks serve as critical reference points for fisheries management, as they define the size window within which reproductive output is maximized before the onset of senescence and the eventual completion of the organismal lifespan at around 9 years [am = around 9 years] at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].
